title: Bamberg Witch Trials: 300 Executed Including Civic Leaders
description: The Bamberg witch trials of 1626–1631 were among the most intense of all European witch persecutions, with approximately 300 people executed in the Prince-Bishopric of Bamberg under Bishop Johann Georg II Fuchs von Dornheim ('the Witch Bishop'). The persecution escalated rapidly from accusations against marginal figures to targeting civic elites: the burgomaster Johannes Junius, the chancellor Dr. Haan, four burgomasters, and the bishop's own chancellor were all executed. The witch house (Malefizhaus) was constructed specifically to hold prisoners. The chain-reaction dynamic — each condemned person naming accomplices under torture — drove the prosecution to levels that would eventually destroy the credibility of the entire enterprise. The trial ended partly through Imperial intervention.
historiographical_note: The Bamberg persecution is central to Wolfgang Behringer's work on German witch-hunting. The fact that accusation chains eventually reached civic leaders and even the bishop's relatives is often cited as evidence of the self-defeating dynamic of torture-driven chain prosecutions. Lyndal Roper in Witch Craze (2004) uses the Bamberg material for her psychoanalytic analysis of accusation patterns.
source_method: Bamberg state archives; Junius letter (1628); secondary scholarship on German witch-hunting
